profile.research_note: [batch narration moved out of reading 2026-09-02] CyrusOne was founded in July 2000 by David Ferdman and Larry Bursten, who had previously built companies acquired by IXC Communications. Wikipedia coverage of CyrusOne states the company opened what it described as the largest data center in Texas in Carrollton in 2012, the anchor of the Dallas Fort Worth cluster that this registry row is part of, alongside CyrusOne buildings in nearby Allen, Lewisville, and Collin County. CyrusOne also operates a substantial San Antonio campus and an Austin facility, both long-running Texas markets for the company, though no specific acquisition or opening story for San Antonio or Austin individually was located in available sourcing this session. The company was acquired by ABRY Partners in 2007, purchased by Cincinnati Bell for 525 million dollars in 2010, completed an IPO in 2013, and was taken private again in 2022 when Kohlberg Kravis Roberts and Global Infrastructure Partners acquired it for 15 billion dollars. No building specific address or individual MW figures were located in available sourcing this session.

reading.body:
CyrusOne's San Antonio campus publishes 9 MW of IT capacity across 110,000 square feet. At a typical AI training density of 40 kW per rack, this suggests roughly 225 racks, well below the scale of dedicated AI training clusters but potentially viable for inference, fine-tuning, or mixed workloads. The facility certifies for regulated data: PCI DSS, HIPAA, ISO 27001, and FISMA compliance, which qualifies it to host financial, healthcare, or government workloads rather than public cloud AI services.

Within Texas, this campus ranks 14th among 18 facilities with published capacity figures, holding 1.9 percent of the state's 468 MW of announced power. Texas has 133 mapped data center locations overall, meaning most publish no specifications. The San Antonio facility represents one node in CyrusOne's multi-city Texas footprint, which includes clusters in the Dallas-Fort Worth corridor and Austin.

At 9 MW, this campus is not a primary constraint on large-scale AI model training and does not signal a shift in compute density toward San Antonio. It matters to AI primarily as part of the regional capacity available for compliance-constrained applications and as an indicator of which markets attract data center capital in Texas. Whether the grid in San Antonio can support significant growth at this site is not published.
